analogy.p: Imagine you send a message to two friends, and each of them sends it to two new friends every 20 minutes. After 1 hour 8 people have it, after 2 hours 64, and after 3 hours 512. That is binary fission: each bacterium 'sends itself' to two cells. The growth is explosive because every new copy also starts copying. The analogy breaks down because real bacteria eventually run out of food and space, so growth slows and stops, whereas a chain letter on paper could in theory carry on.

bullets: A **culture** is a population of microorganisms grown in a laboratory on or in a **culture medium** that supplies nutrients.
An **uncontaminated culture** contains only the intended microorganism, with no unwanted bacteria or fungi mixed in.
Cultures are used to investigate the action of **disinfectants** (chemicals that kill microbes on surfaces) and **antibiotics** (drugs that kill or stop the growth of bacteria inside the body).
Cultures are also used in medicine and industry to identify the bacteria causing an infection, to test new drugs and to grow microorganisms for making products.
Contaminated results are **invalid**: any clear zone or growth could be caused by something other than the test chemical.
This content is **Biology only (triple science)**; combined science students do not need to learn it.
core.p: To **culture** microorganisms means to grow them in controlled conditions so that their numbers increase and can be studied. Scientists need **uncontaminated cultures** - cultures containing only the organism being investigated - to find out how well **disinfectants** and **antibiotics** kill bacteria. If a stray microbe from the air or the student's skin got into the dish, it might grow too, and the results would not show the effect of the chemical being tested. This is why so much of this topic is about **keeping unwanted microorganisms out**.

bullets: Binary fission = one bacterial cell divides into **two identical cells** (asexual reproduction, so the offspring are clones).
Before dividing, the **circular DNA** and the **plasmids** are replicated so each daughter cell gets a full copy of the genetic material.
The cell **elongates**, then the **cell membrane and cell wall** grow inwards at the middle and separate the two cells.
Bacteria can divide **as often as once every 20 minutes** if they have **enough nutrients and a suitable temperature**.
The time for a population to double is called the **mean division time**; it varies with species and conditions.
Because each cell splits into two, the population grows **exponentially**: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 ... not 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
Growth stops in practice when nutrients run out, waste products build up or space runs out, so real cultures cannot double forever.
Link to other topics: because the daughter cells are clones, a **mutation** that gives resistance to an antibiotic is passed on to all descendants (see antibiotic resistance and evolution).
core.p: Bacteria are prokaryotes with no nucleus, so they cannot divide by mitosis. Instead they reproduce by **binary fission**, which the specification calls simple cell division. The bacterial cell first copies its circular chromosome and its plasmids. The cell then grows longer, a new cell wall and membrane form across the middle, and the cell splits into **two genetically identical daughter cells**. Each daughter then repeats the process, so the population doubles every time a cycle is completed.

bullets: **Nutrient broth** is a liquid containing carbohydrates (an energy source), minerals and in some cases proteins or vitamins.
**Agar** is a jelly-like substance made from seaweed, mixed with nutrients and poured into a **Petri dish** where it sets solid.
On agar, each bacterium that lands on the surface divides repeatedly and forms a **colony**, a visible spot made of millions of identical cells.
If the surface is spread evenly with a lot of bacteria the colonies merge into a cloudy **lawn** covering the plate.
Agar is solid, so it does not spill and bacteria stay where they were placed; this lets different test chemicals be placed on different parts of the same plate.
Both media must be **sterilised** before use, otherwise microbes already present would grow and contaminate the culture.
Bacteria in the medium also need oxygen (for most species used in schools), warmth and moisture; these must be suitable for growth.
A **Petri dish** is a shallow, flat, circular dish with a loose lid, made of glass or plastic.
core.h: Culture media: nutrient broth and agar
core.p: Microorganisms need a source of **nutrients** to grow. In the lab these are supplied in a **culture medium**. The specification names two types: **nutrient broth solution**, a liquid, and **agar gel**, a jelly poured into a Petri dish and allowed to set. Each has uses: broth is good for growing large numbers of cells, while agar lets individual bacteria grow into visible **colonies** that can be counted and measured.

bullets: **Sterilise Petri dishes and culture media before use** - to kill any unwanted microorganisms already present (for example in an autoclave using high-pressure steam, or by buying pre-sterilised plastic dishes).

**Sterilise the inoculating loop by passing it through a flame** until it glows red, then let it cool before use - to kill microorganisms on the loop so only the intended bacteria are transferred; cooling prevents the hot loop killing the bacteria you want.
**Inoculating loop** = a wire loop on a handle used to transfer bacteria from one place to the culture medium.
**Secure the lid of the Petri dish with adhesive tape** - to prevent microorganisms from the air entering and to stop the cultured bacteria escaping.
Open the dish lid only as little as needed and for as short a time as possible while transferring bacteria, to reduce the chance of airborne contamination.

Lids are normally taped with a couple of short strips rather than sealed all the way round, so that oxygen can still get in (CLEAPSS safety guidance); this reduces the chance that dangerous anaerobic bacteria grow.
Wash hands, work on a disinfected bench and wipe up spills; this keeps skin and bench microbes out and protects the student.
**Incubate at a suitable temperature** (see the next section) and never open the dish afterwards to look inside.
core.h: Aseptic technique: preparing an uncontaminated culture (Biology only)
core.p: **Aseptic technique** is the set of precautions that stops unwanted microorganisms getting into, or out of, a culture. The specification wants you to be able to **explain** how to prepare an uncontaminated culture, so each step must come with its reason. Mark schemes award a mark for the action and a mark for why it is done. Learn them as pairs: *action* then *purpose*.

bullets: In **school and college laboratories** cultures should generally be incubated at **25 degrees C** to reduce the likelihood of growth of pathogens that might be harmful to humans.
Human body temperature is about **37 degrees C**, which is the ideal temperature for many human pathogens, so 37 degrees C is **not** used in schools.
In **industrial conditions higher temperatures** (often nearer 37 degrees C) can be used because they produce **more rapid growth**; trained staff and strict controls make this safe.
At 25 degrees C growth is slower so schools commonly incubate for around **48 hours**; faster growth in industry saves time and money.
Temperature is a **control variable** in the practical: all plates must be incubated at the same temperature, for the same time.
Too high a temperature would denature the bacteria's enzymes and kill them, so incubators are set below this limit.
Safety link: once cultures have grown, **plates are not opened** and are sterilised or autoclaved before disposal.
core.p: Once the dish is taped, it is placed in an **incubator**, a warm box held at a constant temperature, so that the bacteria grow quickly enough to see in a day or two. The temperature chosen depends on where the work is being done. Higher temperatures make bacteria grow faster because their enzymes work faster, but they also encourage growth of **pathogens**, microorganisms that cause disease in humans. This is a safety trade-off, and the specification expects you to state it.

bullets: **Step 1:** convert the total time and the division time to the **same units** (usually minutes).
**Step 2:** number of divisions = total time / mean division time.
**Step 3:** number of bacteria = starting number x 2 to the power of (number of divisions).
Equation: N = N0 x 2^n, where N0 = starting number of bacteria and n = number of divisions.
Useful powers of 2: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024. Memorise them.
Check your answer is a sensible multiple of the starting number: if n = 3 the population is 8 times bigger.
**Higher tier (HT only):** you may have to express large answers in **standard form**, e.g. 64 000 = 6.4 x 10^4. Use the x 10^n button on a calculator for large powers.
Do not multiply the starting number by the number of divisions; that would be **linear** not exponential growth.
core.h: Calculating the number of bacteria in a population
core.p: You can predict how many bacteria there will be after a given time if you are told the **mean division time**. Work out how many divisions happen, then double the starting number that many times. Because the population doubles, the working uses powers of two. In the examination, always show the number of divisions, since method marks are awarded for this.

bullets: Area of a circle = pi x r^2 (the formula is on the formula sheet in some papers but learn it).
Radius = diameter / 2. The diameter is what you measure with a ruler across the zone, so **halve it first**.
Use pi = 3.14 or the pi button on your calculator, and give the answer to a sensible number of significant figures.
Units of area are **mm^2 or cm^2**. 1 cm^2 = 100 mm^2 because 1 cm = 10 mm and 10 x 10 = 100.
Measure the diameter in two directions at right angles and take a **mean**, since zones are rarely perfect circles.
Measure from the edge of the clear zone, which includes the paper disc (state this is the diameter of the whole clear zone).
The same method works for the cross-sectional area of a **colony** of bacteria.
A common error is to use the diameter as the radius, which makes the area 4 times too big.
core.h: Calculating the area of colonies and clear zones
core.p: A colony or a clear zone is roughly circular on an agar plate, so its **cross-sectional area** is found using the area of a circle. The specification asks for this calculation, and it is used to compare antibiotics. **Area depends on the radius squared**, so a zone with twice the diameter has **four times** the area. This is why comparing area gives a fairer picture of how far the chemical has spread than comparing diameter alone.

bullets: **Method:** use sterile technique to spread a **lawn** of bacteria evenly over a sterilised agar plate (using a sterile spreader or loop).
Use **sterile forceps** to place **filter-paper discs** soaked in different antibiotics or antiseptics (or different concentrations) on the agar, spaced apart.
Include a **control disc** soaked in sterile water (no antibiotic) to show that the paper alone does not stop growth.
Tape the lid on with a couple of strips, label the **base** (not the lid) with names and date, and **incubate at 25 degrees C** for about 48 hours.
After incubation measure the **diameter of each clear zone** in mm with a ruler, then calculate the area with pi x r^2.
**Independent variable:** type (or concentration) of antibiotic/antiseptic. **Dependent variable:** size (diameter/area) of the zone of inhibition.
**Control variables:** same species and amount of bacteria, same depth and type of agar, same size of discs and volume of chemical, same temperature and incubation time.
**Reliability:** repeat on several plates and calculate a mean; **Validity:** only one variable changed and a control used.

**Safety:** wash hands; disinfect the bench; keep dishes taped and never open them after incubation; flame carefully and tie back hair; autoclave dishes before disposal; wear gloves and eye protection if specified.
core.h: Required practical: effect of antiseptics or antibiotics on bacterial growth
core.p: This is the required practical for this topic. The aim is to investigate whether different **antibiotics or antiseptics** stop bacteria growing and to compare how effective they are by measuring the **zone of inhibition** - the clear area around a disc where bacteria have not grown. A bigger zone shows the chemical is more effective at killing or stopping the growth of the bacteria. Exam questions often ask you to describe the method, name variables and explain safety measures.

bullets: A **larger zone** = the chemical is **more effective** at killing or inhibiting that bacterium.
**No zone** = the chemical does not work on these bacteria, or the bacteria are **resistant** to it. The control disc should show no zone.
Zones may differ because the chemical **diffuses at different rates** through agar, so a small zone does not always mean a weak chemical; this is a limitation.
Compare **areas** not just diameters; area is the better measure because it takes account of the whole circle.
A disc with a stronger concentration of the same antibiotic should give a larger zone up to a limit.
Colonies growing **inside** a zone of inhibition suggest some bacteria are **resistant** (they survived and will multiply).
Antibiotics only work against bacteria, **not viruses**, so a test with viruses would show nothing useful.
Antiseptics are used on living tissue (skin); disinfectants are used on surfaces. A test shows effectiveness but not whether the chemical is safe for humans.
core.p: The zone of inhibition is a clear area where the chemical has **diffused** from the disc through the agar and killed bacteria or stopped them dividing. The further the chemical spreads while still strong enough to act, the bigger the clear zone. So the size of the zone is a measure of how effective that chemical is against that species of bacterium. You must be able to compare discs, explain results and suggest conclusions from data tables.

bullets: **Hazard:** pathogenic bacteria may grow. **Risk:** infection. **Control:** incubate at 25 degrees C, tape lid, never open dishes, wash hands.
**Hazard:** Bunsen burner flame. **Risk:** burns or fire. **Control:** tie back hair, keep flammables away, use a safety flame when not heating.
**Hazard:** spills of culture. **Risk:** spreading microbes. **Control:** disinfect the bench before and after work.
**Hazard:** disposal. **Control:** cultures are sterilised by autoclave (high pressure steam) before disposal.
Only use cultures supplied by the teacher/technician; never culture bacteria from your own body or the environment in school.
Antibiotics should be used responsibly in real life: overuse allows resistant strains to evolve (link to evolution by natural selection).
Equipment sterilised by a **disinfectant** or **autoclave** also protects you from your own contamination.
core.p: Culturing bacteria carries real risks because a culture could contain harmful pathogens. A **risk assessment** names a hazard, the risk and the precaution. Exam questions on this topic often ask why the dish is taped or why 25 degrees C is used, which are the same as safety answers. Always give the hazard, the harm that could result and the control measure.

bullets: **Cell biology:** bacteria are prokaryotes; they have DNA free in the cytoplasm and plasmids, no nucleus.
**Infection and response:** antibiotics kill bacterial pathogens; they do not work on viruses; resistance such as **MRSA** is an issue.
**Evolution:** resistant bacteria survive treatment, reproduce and pass on resistance - natural selection.
**Maths skills:** powers of 2, standard form (HT), mean, area of a circle, unit conversion between mm^2 and cm^2.
**Working scientifically:** variables, validity, reliability, risk assessment and drawing conclusions from data.
**Biotechnology:** industrial fermenters culture microorganisms at higher temperatures for faster growth.
**Health:** hospitals sterilise equipment in the same way as the lab - high temperatures and chemical disinfectants.
core.p: This topic links to bacterial structure, antibiotic resistance, how the body fights disease, and calculations. Examiners like questions that combine them, for example, a data table of zones of inhibition followed by a question about natural selection. Make connections between topics explicit in your answers.

bullets: To find the **division time** from data, count how many times the number doubled and divide the total time by that number of doublings.
Large answers must be in standard form: 1 073 741 824 = 1.07 x 10^9 (3 s.f.).
Two plates with the same disc but different zone sizes can mean the plates differ in **agar depth** or **bacterial density**, so these must be controlled.
Explain why a **control** is used: it shows that any clear zone is caused by the antibiotic and not by the paper disc or the agar.
Explain a conclusion carefully: 'Antibiotic B is more effective than A against this bacterium because its zone of inhibition has a greater area'.
Evaluate: results are for one species at 25 degrees C only, so more tests on other bacteria and at body temperature would be needed before claiming it works in patients.
If zone size increases with concentration, plot a graph with concentration on the x axis and zone area on the y axis.
core.h: Higher tier extension and exam-style reasoning
core.p: For top grades you must go beyond description and explain why each step is carried out, and apply the ideas to unfamiliar situations. HT questions often provide a table of time and number of bacteria and ask you to find the mean division time, or give a division time and ask for a standard-form number. Be careful, accurate and show full working.

exam: **Describe/explain aseptic technique (2-4 marks):** give each action AND its reason: 'sterilise Petri dishes and media to kill unwanted microorganisms'; 'pass the loop through a flame to sterilise it'; 'tape the lid to stop microorganisms from the air entering'.

**Why 25 degrees C? (2 marks):** 'to reduce the likelihood of growth of pathogens that might be harmful to humans' (1) and 'higher temperatures (e.g. 37 degrees C) are used in industry for more rapid growth' (1).
**Calculation questions (2-3 marks):** divisions = total time / division time (1); multiply start by 2^n (1); correct answer with units or in standard form (1).
**Area calculations (2-3 marks):** radius = diameter / 2 (1); pi x r^2 (1); answer in mm^2 or cm^2 (1). Show working and the formula.

**Method for zone of inhibition (4-6 marks):** sterile technique, bacterial lawn, discs soaked in different antibiotics with forceps, control disc, tape lid, incubate at 25 degrees C for 48 hours, measure diameter of zones, compare areas.
**Identify variables:** independent = type/concentration of antibiotic; dependent = diameter/area of zone of inhibition; controls = bacteria, agar, disc size, volume, temperature, time.
**Data questions:** use 'larger zone = more effective'; compare using figures from the table ('A has a zone of 14 mm but B has 22 mm'); use both values and units.
**Command words:** 'state' = short fact; 'describe' = what happens; 'explain' = reason using 'because'; 'evaluate' = strengths, weaknesses and a judgement; 'calculate' = numbers with working.
**Standard form (HT):** write answers as a x 10^n with 1 <= a < 10; check by counting the places.
**Safety questions:** state the hazard, then the precaution (e.g. incubate at 25 degrees C so pathogens do not grow well; do not open dishes; autoclave afterwards).
**Graph tips:** time on x axis and number on y axis; the doubling curve is J-shaped (exponential) not a straight line; label axes with units.

mistakes.r: Bacteria divide by binary fission (simple cell division); they have no nucleus.
The lid is taped to prevent microorganisms from the air entering (and cultured bacteria escaping); it is not sealed completely.
mistakes.w: The lid is taped on to stop air getting into the dish and the bacteria suffocating.

mistakes.r: The inoculating loop is passed through a flame to sterilise it and kill unwanted microorganisms.
mistakes.w: The loop is put in a flame to warm it up for the bacteria.

mistakes.r: In schools cultures are incubated at about 25 degrees C to reduce the chance of growing human pathogens; higher temperatures are used industrially for faster growth.
mistakes.w: School cultures are kept at 37 degrees C because that is best for bacteria.

mistakes.r: Radius = half the diameter; then area = pi x r^2.
mistakes.w: Using the diameter as the radius in pi r squared.

mistakes.r: A larger zone of inhibition means the antibiotic/antiseptic is more effective at killing or preventing growth of the bacteria.
mistakes.w: A bigger zone is caused by a stronger drug so the bacteria are stronger.

mistakes.r: A control disc with sterile water shows the clear zone is caused by the antibiotic and not by the disc or agar.
mistakes.w: The antibiotic killed the bacteria so a clear zone appears with no explanation about the control.

mistakes.r: Number of bacteria = start number x 2^(number of divisions), because the population doubles each time.
mistakes.w: Number of bacteria = start number x number of divisions.

mistakes.r: Antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses.

summary: You must know how bacteria multiply by binary fission, how uncontaminated cultures are grown on agar plates or in broth using aseptic technique, how to calculate population size and the area of colonies or clear zones, and how to carry out the required practical on antiseptics and antibiotics (Biology only). It matters because every test of a new antibiotic or disinfectant depends on cultures that contain only the microorganism you meant to grow.

terms.d: A population of microorganisms grown in the laboratory on or in a culture medium.
A substance containing nutrients in which microorganisms are grown, for example nutrient broth or agar gel.
A liquid culture medium containing nutrients for the growth of microorganisms.
A jelly-like culture medium, set in a Petri dish, on which colonies of bacteria can be grown.
Simple cell division in which a bacterial cell divides into two identical cells; it can happen as often as once every 20 minutes.
The average time taken for a population of bacteria to double in number.
A visible group of identical bacteria that has grown from a single bacterium on an agar plate.
Methods used to prevent unwanted microorganisms contaminating a culture, for example sterilising equipment and taping the lid.
A culture containing only the microorganism being investigated.
To kill all microorganisms on equipment or in media, for example by heating in an autoclave or passing through a flame.
A wire loop used to transfer microorganisms to a culture medium; sterilised by passing it through a flame.
To keep a culture at a controlled temperature so that microorganisms can grow; 25 degrees C in schools.
A drug that kills bacteria or prevents their growth inside the body; does not work against viruses.
A chemical applied to skin or living tissue to kill microorganisms or stop their growth.
A chemical that kills microorganisms on non-living surfaces.
The clear area around a disc on an agar plate where bacterial growth has been prevented by the chemical.
A disc with no antibiotic (e.g. sterile water) used to show that the disc itself does not stop bacterial growth.

worked.q: One bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are there after 2 hours? (2 marks)
A food sample contains 250 bacteria. The mean division time is 30 minutes. Calculate the number of bacteria after 4 hours. Give your answer in standard form. (3 marks, HT)

worked.ans: A = 154 mm^2, B = 380 mm^2. Antibiotic B is more effective because its zone of inhibition is larger.
worked.q: On an agar plate disc A gave a clear zone of diameter 14 mm and disc B a zone of diameter 22 mm. Calculate the area of each zone and say which antibiotic is more effective. (4 marks)
steps: A: radius = 14 / 2 = 7 mm; area = pi x 7^2 = pi x 49 = 153.9 mm^2 (about 154 mm^2).
B: radius = 22 / 2 = 11 mm; area = pi x 11^2 = pi x 121 = 380.1 mm^2 (about 380 mm^2).
B's area is about 2.5 times that of A (121 / 49 = 2.47).
A larger zone of inhibition shows the antibiotic is more effective.
